\chapter{Setting Off --- The Way Out, the Journey, the Return, the Arrival, the Farewell}
\label{ch:la-partida}
\hlchaptermodality{288}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the way out, the journey, the return, the arrival and the farewell in Spanish.}

Complete ES-C288-despedida: name all five stages of a departure in order, from the way out to the goodbye.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la salida]{la salida — the Romans jumped out of rooms}

\label{lesson:ES-C288-salida}



\begin{quote}
Before a new run: what does \emph{platys} mean? (Flat.) And what is a \emph{cochlea}? (A snail shell.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item salir — the word this one is made from.
  \item la puerta — where the way out generally is.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sa-LI-da}, stress on the \emph{li}. The \emph{d} between vowels is soft, close to the \emph{th} of \emph{this}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la salida} — \textquotedblleft{}the exit,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the way out.\textquotedblright{}

From \textbf{salir}, which you have, and behind \emph{salir} is Latin \textbf{salire}, to jump. A Roman did not leave a room; he jumped out of it. It calmed down on its way into Spanish and kept only the departing.

The jumping survives in the English loans. Something \textbf{salient} is jumping out at you. An \textbf{assault} is a jumping-at. A \textbf{somersault} is a jump over the top. And to \textbf{sally} out of a fort is the same word once more, arriving through French.

The ending is worth as much as the root. \emph{-ida} on an action gives you the act or the result of it, and it is going to give you three of the next four words.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You have had \emph{salir} for a long time; now you have the name of what it does.

That is a cheap way to grow a vocabulary, and Spanish is unusually generous with it. A word you know plus an ending you know is a word you did not have to learn.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la salida}
  \item \emph{salir}, then \emph{la salida}, and hear the first one inside the second
  \item \emph{la puerta de salida}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{salire} mean? (To jump.) What does the \emph{-ida} ending do? (Turns an action into the act or the result.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el viaje]{el viaje — the packed lunch that became the journey}

\label{lesson:ES-C288-viaje}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{salire} mean? (To jump.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la salida — how this one begins.
  \item caminar — the walking you already have.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{VIA-je}, stress on the first syllable. The \emph{j} is the \emph{jota}, and the \emph{ia} is one glide. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el viaje} — \textquotedblleft{}the journey.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{viaticum}, from \textbf{via}, a road: not the journey at all, but the money and food you packed for one. Spanish moved the word off the supplies and onto the trip.

English took the same \emph{viaticum} through French and got \textbf{voyage}. It also has \emph{via} on its own: a \textbf{viaduct} carries a road; something \textbf{trivial} is \emph{tri-via}, the place where three roads meet, and what gets said at a crossroads is not important.

The shift is the interesting part. A word for the preparation became the word for the thing prepared for. That happens constantly, and it is why so many ordinary words look sideways at their own meaning.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two of the five, and both were something else first.

A jump became a way out; a packed bag became a journey. Neither word describes what it now names.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el viaje}
  \item \emph{buen viaje}
  \item \emph{la salida} and \emph{el viaje}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was a \emph{viaticum}? (The provisions for a road.) Which English word is the same one? (\emph{Voyage}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la vuelta]{la vuelta — everything here is rolling}

\label{lesson:ES-C288-vuelta}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what was a \emph{viaticum}? (The provisions for a road.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el viaje — what this one ends.
  \item la puerta — where you first met the \emph{o} opening into \emph{ue}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{VUEL-ta}, stress on the first syllable. The \emph{ue} is one glide and the \emph{l} stays clear. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la vuelta} — \textquotedblleft{}the return,\textquotedblright{} and also a turn.

From \textbf{volver}, Latin \textbf{volvere}, to roll or turn. The stressed \emph{o} opens into \emph{ue} exactly as you now expect it to: \emph{volta} to \emph{vuelta}, as \emph{portam} went to \emph{puerta}.

\textbf{Volvere} rolled a long way into English. To \textbf{revolve} is to roll again. A \textbf{revolution} is one full turn — of a wheel first and of a state a great deal later. And a \textbf{volume} is a rolled-up scroll, which is why a book carries the same name as a quantity of space.

\emph{Vuelta} is not only a return. It is a lap of a track, a turn of a key, and change handed back in a shop. All of them are the same rolling, and Spanish did not bother to invent separate words.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now predict this vowel rather than memorise it.

\emph{Puerta}, \emph{cierto}, \emph{fiebre}, \emph{vuelta}: stressed \emph{o} to \emph{ue}, stressed \emph{e} to \emph{ie}. Given a Latin word you have never seen, you can guess the Spanish — and be right more often than not.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la vuelta}
  \item \emph{volver}, then \emph{la vuelta}
  \item \emph{la salida}, \emph{el viaje}, \emph{la vuelta}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{volvere} mean? (To roll or turn.) Why is a book a \emph{volume}? (Because it was a rolled scroll.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la llegada]{la llegada — the sails are folded, so you have arrived}

\label{lesson:ES-C288-llegada}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what does \emph{volvere} mean? (To roll or turn.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la vuelta — the return this one completes.
  \item cl-, pl-, fl- $\to$ ll- — the change you are about to see happen.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{lle-GA-da}, stress on the \emph{ga}. The \emph{ll} is a \emph{y} sound for most speakers, and the \emph{g} before \emph{a} is hard. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la llegada} — \textquotedblleft{}the arrival.\textquotedblright{}

From \textbf{llegar}, to arrive, and this is the best story of the five. Latin \textbf{plicare} means to fold. A ship coming in to shore folded its sails — \emph{plicare vela} — and the phrase wore down until the folding meant the arriving and the sails were gone from the sentence entirely.

Now the beginning of the word. \emph{Plicare} to \emph{llegar}: the \emph{pl-} has become \emph{ll-}, which is the change you have already met by name and can now watch doing real work.

\textbf{Ply}, \textbf{apply}, \textbf{complicate}, and a \textbf{plait} are the English relatives, every one of them still folding something. \emph{Complicate} is to fold together, which is a fair description of what it does to a plan.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A sound change you learned as a rule has just paid for itself.

You did not have to be told that \emph{llegar} comes from \emph{plicare}; the \emph{ll-} at the front told you it came from something with \emph{pl-}. Rules about sound are worth more than lists of words, because they work on words you have never met.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la llegada}
  \item \emph{plicare}, then \emph{llegar}, and hear the \emph{pl-} collapse
  \item \emph{la salida} and \emph{la llegada}, the two ends of a trip
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{plicare} mean? (To fold.) What was being folded? (The sails of a ship coming in.) What happened to the \emph{pl-}? (It became \emph{ll-}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la despedida]{la despedida — taking your leave was asking for it}

\label{lesson:ES-C288-despedida}



\begin{quote}
Before the last of the five: what did \emph{plicare} mean? (To fold.) And what did \emph{salire} mean? (To jump.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item adiós — one thing you say at this moment.
  \item hasta luego — and another.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{des-pe-DI-da}, stress on the \emph{di}. Both \emph{d} sounds between vowels are soft. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la despedida} — \textquotedblleft{}the farewell,\textquotedblright{} the act of saying goodbye.

From \textbf{despedir}, and behind it Latin \textbf{expetere}: \emph{ex-}, out, plus \textbf{petere}, to seek or to ask. To take your leave was to ask for it — which is still what a leave-taking is, underneath the politeness.

\textbf{Petere} is a large family in English. A \textbf{petition} asks. To \textbf{compete} is to seek alongside somebody. An \textbf{appetite} seeks towards. And to \textbf{repeat} is to seek a thing again.

\emph{Adiós}, \emph{hasta luego} and \emph{hasta mañana} have been yours since near the start, and you have been saying them without a word for the act itself. This is that word.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \emph{la salida}, \emph{el viaje}, \emph{la vuelta}, \emph{la llegada}, \emph{la despedida}.

Set out in order they trace a whole departure — the way out, the journey, the return, the arrival, and the goodbye that opens the whole thing. Four of the five are words you already had, wearing an ending. Only the endings were new.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la despedida}
  \item \emph{adiós}, then \emph{la despedida} — the word and the act
  \item all five in order — \emph{la salida}, \emph{el viaje}, \emph{la vuelta}, \emph{la llegada}, \emph{la despedida}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the pieces of \emph{expetere}? (\emph{Ex-}, out, and \emph{petere}, to ask.) Which English words still ask? (\emph{Petition}, \emph{compete}, \emph{appetite}, \emph{repeat}.) And what did \emph{plicare} mean? (To fold.)
\end{tcolorbox}
